source.title: Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws
source.authors: Nikhil Sardana; Jacob Portes; Sasha Doubov; Jonathan Frankle

record.file_problem: The full paper is present; no material truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests loss behaviour at extreme training-token ratios and how well Chinchilla-style fits extrapolate there; it reports that loss keeps improving but that the original fitting approach overpredicts the benefits of additional data and can fit the extreme-run results poorly.
record.gate_note: The paper's inference-adjusted optimal allocations are computed using an assumed Chinchilla loss function, not empirically tested against observed optimal allocations. The paper also discusses results from other studies; those cited findings are not recorded as rows. The experimental sweep measures loss and downstream metrics across token-to-parameter ratios, not isolated parameter-count or compute scaling.
record.test_reason: The study trains 47 MPT models (150M–6B, 10–10,000 tokens/param). It refits the Chinchilla parametric law on growing subsets of runs and argues that typical-ratio fits overestimate the gains from extra data at extreme ratios. It also finds the parametric form cannot fit the 150M long-ratio runs. That is a specific argument that V2 and V7 need qualifying. Its inference-adjusted allocation analysis uses assumed Chinchilla coefficients and is not a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it omits the paper's main contribution. Modifying Chinchilla laws to include inference cost, practitioners expecting large inference demand (~1B requests) should train models smaller and longer than Chinchilla-optimal, in both FLOPs and dollar cost. Experiments show loss and the Gauntlet Average keep improving up to 10,000 tok/param without saturation. Chinchilla-style fits from typical ratios overestimate the gains from extra data at extreme ratios.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the Chinchilla parametric loss form and fitting procedure, with MPT models trained on a different dataset and architecture and with experiments extended to much higher token-to-parameter ratios. The paper uses L-BFGS, grid initialisations and Huber loss for its fits.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted coefficients and curve shape vary with the maximum token-to-parameter ratio included in the fitting data. The paper also reports poorer fit for the 150M model's long-ratio results.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss shows no saturation up to 10,000 tok/param for 150M, contrary to De Vries's critical-model-size hypothesis.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small models keep improving in loss with no plateau at extreme token-to-parameter ratios.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 235, 2024)
record.problems: Only 47 training runs were collected, compared with over 400 in the Chinchilla study; model sizes reach 6B rather than 16B. The sweep is incomplete for several model sizes, and the paper notes resource constraints. Reported experimental trends are largely shown in figures without numerical values or uncertainty intervals. The 6B model has only the 20-token-per-parameter run listed in Table 4.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows left out. The 6B run is retained as a cannot-determine result because it has no token-ratio sweep.

untested.parts: Power law in parameters at non-bottleneck data. Loss-vs-tokens form, which is not readable. Range is limited to 150M–6B.
Extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger in parameters or compute. Only token-ratio extrapolation is examined, without quantified prediction errors.
Not tested empirically. Allocations are computed from assumed Chinchilla coefficients.
Not tested; shape is not varied at fixed N.
Not tested; text only, single epoch, no repeated data, no fine-tuning.
Individual-task predictability and other model families.
Parameter counting, schedule, dataset and alternative fitting methods are not varied.

missing.what: Per-category Gauntlet results: less consistent correlation with data and model size; near-zero accuracy on Symbolic Problem Solving.
missing.locator: Section 4 last paragraph; Appendix D; Figure 7

missing.what: Training at <20 tokens/param is less compute-efficient, which the authors say agrees with Chinchilla. This bears weakly on the ~20 tok/param optimum.
Statement that models at extreme durations learn more slowly than the scaling laws predict. This is the ≤100 fit's extrapolation, shown only in Figure 5 with no error numbers.

record.verdict_notes: The Section 2/6 allocation results (Tables 2–3) are computed from assumed Chinchilla coefficients and are not tests of V3. The loss is smoothed final training loss in a single epoch, so it is close to held-out. Only 47 runs; no uncertainty is reported. Most trends are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss as training tokens per parameter increase, including extreme ratios. Does not isolate token count while holding other factors in the version's stated non-bottleneck regime, or test power-law scaling in parameters and compute.
Tests whether fits from typical token-to-parameter ratios extrapolate to very long training durations. Does not test predicting runs orders of magnitude larger in parameter count or compute.

The paper calculates inference-adjusted choices using an assumed loss law; it does not empirically test whether the fixed-compute loss-minimising parameter and token counts follow stable powers of compute.
Architecture details are not varied at a fixed parameter count.
The experiments concern text pretraining without repeated data; other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested.
Tests the relationship between pretraining loss, token-to-parameter ratio and the paper's Evaluation Gauntlet metrics. Does not test predictability on every downstream task or other model families.

Tests fitting-data cutoff and extreme token-ratio effects with the paper's chosen architecture, data, training procedure and fitting method. Does not systematically vary parameter counting, schedules, datasets, or alternative fitting methods.
